fields.Front: What is the key difference between a message queue and pub/sub?
fields.Back: A queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer (point-to-point); pub/sub broadcasts each message to every subscriber of a topic.

fields.Front: Give an example use case better suited to a message queue than pub/sub.
fields.Back: Distributing work items across a pool of workers, where each task should be processed by only one worker (e.g. a background job queue).

fields.Front: Give an example use case better suited to pub/sub than a message queue.
fields.Back: Broadcasting an event (e.g. 'order placed') to multiple independent services that each need to react — email, analytics, inventory.

fields.Front: In Kafka, what is a topic?
fields.Back: A named stream/category of messages that producers write to and consumers read from.

fields.Front: In Kafka, what is a partition?
fields.Back: A topic is split into ordered, append-only partitions, each of which can be processed independently to allow parallelism.

fields.Front: In Kafka, what is an offset?
fields.Back: A sequential id marking a message's position within a partition, used by consumers to track their read progress.

fields.Front: In Kafka, what is a consumer group?
fields.Back: A set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic, where each partition is consumed by only one consumer in the group at a time.

fields.Front: Why does Kafka only guarantee message ordering within a partition, not across a whole topic?
fields.Back: Partitions are processed independently and in parallel by different consumers, so there's no global order across them — only within each partition's own sequence.

fields.Front: Why is 'at-least-once' delivery the most common choice in practice, even though it can duplicate messages?
fields.Back: It's simpler and cheaper to guarantee than exactly-once; the duplication risk is handled by making the consumer's handler idempotent.

fields.Front: What does it mean for a message handler to be idempotent?
fields.Back: Processing the same message multiple times produces the same result as processing it once, with no duplicate side effects.

fields.Front: Give a common technique to make an operation idempotent.
fields.Back: Use a unique idempotency key (e.g. request or message id), and check/record it before applying the operation, skipping it if already processed.
A separate queue that messages are routed to after repeatedly failing processing, so they don't block the main queue and can be inspected or retried later.

fields.Front: What is backpressure in a messaging system?
fields.Back: A mechanism that slows or pauses producers when consumers can't keep up, preventing the system from being overwhelmed.

fields.Front: Name one way a system can apply backpressure.
fields.Back: Bounded queues that block or reject new messages once full, or pull-based consumers that explicitly request a limited batch size.
Storing all changes to application state as an immutable sequence of events, rather than just the current state, so state is derived by replaying events.

fields.Front: What is a key benefit of event sourcing?
fields.Back: A full audit log/history of how state was reached, plus the ability to rebuild or replay state as of any point in time.

fields.Front: Why is CQRS often paired with event sourcing?
fields.Back: Events from the write model naturally serve as the source of truth used to build and update optimized read-side projections.

fields.Front: What is the tradeoff between synchronous (request/response) and asynchronous (event/message-based) service communication?
fields.Back: Sync is simpler and gives an immediate result but couples services' availability and latency together; async decouples services and improves resilience/throughput but adds complexity (eventual consistency, harder debugging).

fields.Front: Why can strict message ordering be hard to achieve at scale?
fields.Back: Parallelism (multiple partitions/consumers) is needed for throughput, but processing in parallel breaks global order — ordering is usually only guaranteed per-partition or per-key.

fields.Text: Message delivery semantics: {{c1::at-most-once}} (message may be lost, never duplicated), {{c2::at-least-once}} (message may be duplicated, never lost), {{c3::exactly-once}} (message delivered and processed exactly one time).
CQRS separates the {{c1::write model}} (handles commands that change state) from the {{c2::read model}} (optimized for queries), often backed by different data stores.
